essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to write a basic technical report, from gathering the facts to handing it in.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find out why the report is needed, who will read it and when it is due. Then I gather the facts while they are fresh: I make notes, take measurements and readings, take photos and ask witnesses what they saw. I use who, what, when, where, why and how to make sure nothing is missed. Next I plan the headings, such as introduction, findings, conclusion and recommendations, and sort my notes under each one. I write a first draft in short, plain sentences, with units on every measurement and tables or photos where they help. I read the draft through, check the facts, figures and spelling, and ask my supervisor or a co-worker to check it. Finally I sign and date it, hand it to the person who asked for it, and save or file a copy.
markingPoints: Finds out the purpose, the reader and the deadline
Gathers facts at the time: notes, measurements, photos, witnesses
Plans the headings and sorts the information
Writes a clear draft and then checks it, with a second reader
Signs, dates, hands in and files a copy

essays.stem: Describe the main parts of a basic technical report and what goes in each part.
essays.modelAnswer: A report starts with a title, the date, the writer's name and the name of the person it is for, and often a job number. The introduction says why the report was written and what it covers, for example "An inspection of the welding bay on 20 October". The findings or details section gives the facts: what was seen, measured or tested, with units, and with tables, sketches or photos where they help. The conclusion sums up what the findings mean, such as "Two of the six machines are not safe to use". The recommendations say what should be done next, by whom and by when. Some reports also have a short summary at the start and an appendix at the end for test sheets or other papers. The report ends with the writer's signature.
markingPoints: Title, date, writer, reader and job number
Introduction: purpose and what the report covers
Findings: facts, measurements, tables and photos
Conclusion: what the findings mean
Recommendations: actions, by whom and when (summary, appendix, signature as extras)

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a fact and an opinion, and why technical reports should be based on facts. Give an example of each from your trade.
essays.modelAnswer: A fact is something that can be seen, measured or checked, and it is the same no matter who writes it down. An opinion is what a person thinks or feels, and another person may think differently. For example, "The fillet weld on the bracket has a leg length of 4 mm, but the drawing asks for 6 mm" is a fact, because anyone can measure it. "The welder did a poor job" is an opinion. In electrical work, "The socket outlet in the kitchen has a cracked cover" is a fact, while "The wiring looks old and dodgy" is an opinion. Reports are used to make decisions about safety, money and repairs, so they must be based on facts that can be checked. If an opinion is needed, for example an expert view, it should be clearly marked as an opinion and backed by the facts.
markingPoints: A fact can be seen, measured or checked
An opinion is what a person thinks or feels
Gives a correct example of a fact from the trade
Gives a correct example of an opinion
Explains that decisions depend on facts; opinions are marked and backed by facts

essays.stem: A trainee gets a small burn from hot metal in the workshop. Describe what information the incident report should contain.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should give the name of the injured trainee and the name of the person writing the report. It should give the date, the time and the exact place, such as "Welding bay 3". It should describe what happened in plain words and in the order it happened: what the trainee was doing, what equipment and PPE they were using, and how the burn happened. It should describe the injury, for example "a small burn on the back of the left hand", and say what first aid was given and by whom, such as cooling the burn under cool running water. It should list any witnesses and what they saw. It should say what was done straight away to make the area safe, and recommend how to stop it happening again, such as wearing gauntlets. The report is signed, dated and given to the supervisor quickly.
markingPoints: Names, date, time and exact place
What happened, in order, with the task, equipment and PPE
The injury and the first aid given, and by whom
Witnesses and immediate actions taken
Recommendations to prevent it happening again; signed and handed in quickly

essays.stem: Explain how to write a report in clear, plain language that the reader can understand easily.
essays.modelAnswer: I think about who will read the report, such as a supervisor, a customer or an inspector, and choose words that suit them. I use short sentences and everyday words, with one idea in each sentence. I say exactly what I mean, for example "the gate hinge is cracked" rather than "there is a problem with the gate". I give exact numbers with units, such as 230 V or 6 mm, and exact dates and times. If I must use a trade word or an abbreviation, I explain it or write it out in full the first time. I keep to the facts and leave out my feelings. I use headings, numbered points and tables so that the reader can find things quickly. I keep the report as short as it can be while still giving all the facts. At the end I read it again as if I were the reader.
markingPoints: Thinks about the reader and chooses suitable words
Short sentences, everyday words, one idea per sentence
Exact facts, numbers with units, dates and times
Explains trade terms and abbreviations the first time
Uses headings, points and tables; keeps it short; re-reads as the reader

essays.stem: Explain how photos, tables and sketches can improve a technical report, and how each one should be used.
essays.modelAnswer: Photos show the reader exactly what was found, such as a cracked weld or a burnt cable, so there is less chance of misunderstanding. Each photo should be clear and close enough to show the detail, with something to show the size, such as a rule, and a caption saying what it shows, where and when it was taken. Photos of people should only be taken with their permission. Tables are used when there are many items or readings, such as ten fire extinguishers or a set of test results. A table with clear column headings and units lets the reader compare items quickly. Sketches show positions, shapes and sizes, such as where a leaking pipe is in a room or the shape of a broken bracket. They should be neat, labelled and have the main sizes. Each one should be numbered and referred to in the text.
markingPoints: Photos show exactly what was found
Photos: clear, with a size reference and a caption; permission for people
Tables: for many items or readings, with headings and units
Sketches: for positions, shapes and sizes, labelled
Each is numbered and referred to in the text

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a simple safety inspection of a workshop area and write a report on it.
essays.modelAnswer: I agree with my supervisor which area to inspect and get the inspection checklist. I wear the right PPE for the area. I walk through the area and look at each item on the list, such as fire extinguishers, the first-aid box, exits and walkways, extension leads and plugs, machine guards, gas cylinders and housekeeping. I only look and do not open or repair anything. I write down what I find at the time, with the place and the condition of each item, and take photos of any problems. If I find a serious danger, I report it to my supervisor straight away and do not wait for the report. Then I write the report: an introduction with the area, date and purpose, a table of findings, a conclusion and clear recommendations saying what must be done and by whom. I sign, date and hand it in.
markingPoints: Agrees the area and uses a checklist, with the right PPE
Checks each item by looking only, and records findings and photos at the time
Reports serious dangers straight away
Writes the report: introduction, findings table, conclusion
Gives clear recommendations; signs, dates and hands it in

essays.stem: Describe how you would check a report before you hand it in.
essays.modelAnswer: I leave the report for a short time if I can, then read it through slowly from start to finish. I check that it answers the question I was asked and has all the parts, such as the introduction, findings, conclusion and recommendations. I check every fact, measurement and reading against my notes, and make sure each number has its unit. I check that the names, dates, times and job numbers are right. I look for any opinion that should be left out or marked clearly as an opinion. I check the spelling and grammar, using a spell checker or dictionary for trade words. I make sure every photo, table and sketch is labelled and in the right place. Then I ask my supervisor or a co-worker to read it, because another person often sees mistakes that I miss. Last, I sign and date it.
markingPoints: Reads it through and checks it answers the brief and has all parts
Checks facts, figures and units against the notes
Checks names, dates, times and job numbers
Checks spelling, grammar, labels on photos and tables
Has a second person check it, then signs and dates it

essays.stem: Explain why reports must be accurate, honest and kept secure, and describe how you would store paper and digital reports.
essays.modelAnswer: Reports are used to make decisions about safety, repairs and money, so a wrong or dishonest report can lead to someone getting hurt, money being wasted or the business being blamed. A report may also be needed later as evidence, for example if there is a complaint, an insurance claim or an accident inquiry, so it must show what really happened. Reports often hold private details about customers, staff and prices, so they must be kept secure and shared only with people who need them. Paper reports should be filed in the right folder by date or job number, in a cabinet that can be locked, and kept for the time the business decides. Digital reports should be saved with a clear file name in the agreed work folder, protected by a password and backed up. They should never be posted on personal social media.
markingPoints: Decisions on safety, repairs and money depend on accurate reports
Reports may be needed later as evidence
Private details must be kept secure and shared only as needed
Paper: filed by date or job number in a lockable cabinet, kept for the set time
Digital: clear file names, agreed folder, password, backup, not on social media

essays.stem: Describe what you would include in a job completion report for a customer after fitting a steel gate or installing outdoor security lights.
essays.modelAnswer: The report would start with the business name, the customer's name and address, the job number and the date the work was finished. I would describe the work that was done in plain words, for example "Fitted one double steel gate, 3 m wide, with two drop bolts and a padlock bracket" or "Installed four outdoor LED security lights with a light sensor on the front and side walls". I would list the main materials used and say if anything was different from the quotation, and why. For electrical work I would say that the work was tested and attach or refer to the test record. I would note any problems found, such as a weak wall or an old cable, and give advice on care, such as painting the gate or keeping sensors clean. I would add the warranty details, and leave space for the customer to sign that the work is complete.
markingPoints: Business and customer details, job number and date
Clear description of the work done
Materials used and any changes from the quote, with reasons
Tests done (for electrical work) and any problems found
Care advice, warranty and the customer's signature

practical1.title: Carry out a workshop safety inspection and write an inspection report
practical1.brief: The assessor chooses one area of the Centre for your group to inspect, such as the welding bay or the electrical workshop, and gives you an inspection checklist. As a group, plan the inspection and share the area so that each member inspects one part (for example fire safety and exits, the first-aid box and PPE, extension leads and plugs, machines and guards, gas cylinders and housekeeping). This is a look-only inspection: do not open, switch on, adjust or repair anything. Each member records their findings at the time and takes photos with captions. Then, together, write one inspection report with a title, an introduction, a table of findings, a conclusion and numbered recommendations. Each member writes the findings for their part and at least one recommendation, and one member checks the whole report before all members sign it. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the report once for the whole group.
materials: The inspection checklist for the chosen area
A phone or tablet for photos (with the assessor's permission)
A report template, on paper or on a computer
Safety boots, safety glasses and any other PPE the area needs
photos: The group planning the inspection, with the area shared out on the checklist
Members inspecting their parts of the area (look only)
Photos of at least three findings, each with a caption
The report signed by every member
checklist: Took part in planning and knew which part they were inspecting
Wore the right PPE and inspected by looking only
Recorded findings at the time, with place, item and condition
Took clear photos with captions saying what, where and when
Wrote their findings in plain, factual sentences with correct units
Wrote at least one clear recommendation saying what, who and when
Reported any serious danger to the assessor straight away
Checked the report and signed it
safety: Look only: do not open, switch on, adjust or repair any equipment
Do not touch gas cylinder valves or electrical panels
Keep out of welding booths that are in use, and keep away from moving machines
Report any serious danger to the assessor at once
Take photos only of equipment and places, not of people without their permission

practical2.title: Investigate a staged near miss and write an incident report
practical2.brief: The assessor sets up a staged near-miss scene in the workshop, for example a trailing extension lead (unplugged) across a walkway, a spilled patch of oil near a bench and a tool left on the edge of a ladder. One person (a member or the assessor) plays a witness, using a script from the assessor. As a group, investigate as you would after a real near miss. Photograph and measure the scene before anything is moved, make a labelled sketch, and interview the witness, writing down what they say in their own words. Then complete the Centre's incident or near-miss form and write a short incident report with the facts in time order, the causes and numbered recommendations. Swap roles so that every member does at least two of these jobs: photographing, measuring and sketching, interviewing, filling in the form, and writing a part of the report. Read the finished report to the assessor as if they were your supervisor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: The staged scene set up by the assessor (all equipment unplugged and safe)
The witness script (for the witness only)
The Centre's incident or near-miss report form
Clipboards, pens, paper and a 5 m tape measure
A phone or tablet for photos (with the assessor's permission)
photos: The scene before anything was moved, from two directions
The labelled sketch of the scene
The witness interview, with the notes being written
The completed incident or near-miss form
The finished report being read to the assessor
checklist: Photographed and measured the scene before anything was moved
Made or helped make a neat, labelled sketch with sizes
Asked the witness open questions and wrote their words without changing them
Kept to facts and did not blame anyone in the report
Gave the date, time, place and events in the correct order
Named the causes and wrote clear recommendations to stop it happening again
Filled in every box of the form, using N/A where a box did not apply
Took part in at least two roles and spoke clearly when reporting to the assessor
safety: The scene is staged: keep all leads unplugged and do not switch anything on
Do not step in the spilled liquid; keep to the marked route round the scene
Do not climb the ladder in the scene
Wear safety boots in the workshop, and clean up the scene with the assessor at the end
